title: MoE routing load imbalance and attention sparsity operational notes
body:
Summary:

This doc captures a set of experiments and heuristics we ran to understand why MoE-backed models show high token-level tail latency and memory churn compared to dense variants (Llama/Mistral/Qwen) when serving long-context workloads. It also records early experiments with attention sparsity (sliding windows / block-sparse attention) on Qwen and Mistral families and how those interact with routing and memory allocation patterns.

High-level findings:
- MoE routing overhead is dominated not by the gate MLP FLOPs, but by the scatter/gather, per-expert buffer allocation, and host-GPU synchronization that accompanies routing maps. Measured gate compute ~6% of runtime, scatter/gather/memcpy ~20–30% depending on batch size and expert count.
- For short sequences (<256 tokens) routing overhead is proportionally large: p95 per-token latency increases ~2–3x vs dense because of fixed per-request routing book-keeping. For long sequences (>2k tokens), overhead amortizes but memory fragmentation becomes visible: repeated expert swaps cause CUDA allocator churn.
- Attention sparsity experiments on Qwen (sliding-window + global tokens) reduce compute but increase memory working set due to intermediate sparse index buffers and tiled GEMM scheduling; net win only when seq_len > 4k and using fused kernels.
- Tokenization differences between models (byte-pair boundary placement) change effective sequence length distribution and can alter batching efficiency—important when comparing Llama vs Qwen for same text corpus.

Testbed & measurement setup:
- Hardware: 1x A100-80GB (but we ran microbenchmarks on both A100-40GB and H100 instances for compiler differences).
- Serving runtime: local branch profiling-mode (git PR 1348) with the routing instrumentation flag enabled.
- Models tested: Llama-2-13B (dense), Mistral-7B-v0.1 (dense), Qwen-7B-1.2 (long-context variant), MoE-28B (top-2 gating, 64 experts).
- Input distribution: mixture of ~60% short (<=128 tokens), 30% medium (512–2048), 10% long (>=4096) sequences sampled from customer telemetry (anonymized).
- Tools: torch.profiler (CPU+CUDA), Nsight Systems timeline captures, ncu for kernel-level breakdown, and custom logging of route maps and expert id distributions per-batch.

Representative numbers (median over 10 runs, single request throughput, mixed batch sizes aggregated):
- Llama-2-13B, seq=512: tokens/sec 2200, p95 per-token latency 6.1ms, GPU mem 12.3GB
- Mistral-7B, seq=2048: tokens/sec 1450, p95 per-token latency 8.9ms, GPU mem 9.1GB
- Qwen-7B (sliding-window attention, seq=8192): tokens/sec 720, p95 per-token latency 18.3ms, GPU mem 14.7GB
- MoE-28B (top-2, 64 experts), seq=2048: tokens/sec 560, p95 per-token latency 34.2ms, GPU mem 22.1GB
- MoE routing overhead breakdown (measured): gate MLP 6% | compute remapping + scatter/gather 22% | memory allocations & syncs 12% | remaining model compute 60%

Profiling traces & observations:
- Timeline shows frequent small memcpy H2D/D2H around routing stage when expert outputs are consolidated. These appear as many small memcpy ops on the timeline, interleaved with kernels, causing kernel launch stalls.
- nsight stack: high number of cudaMalloc/cudaFree calls when using default allocator per-request. Using a pre-allocated pool reduces p95 by ~18% for MoE tests.
- Kernel launch counts: for MoE top-2 with micro-batch of 1, kernel launches per token ~120 (vs ~40 for dense). Launch overhead and per-launch latency dominate for short sequences.
- Attention sparsity (Qwen sliding-window): when using fused Triton kernels for block-sparse matmuls we see 30–45% throughput improvement vs naïve sparse implementation. Without fusion, index scatter overhead negates compute savings.

Root cause hypotheses (ranked):
1) Memory allocator churn and small-memcopy patterns from scatter/gather are the dominant practical cost.
2) Per-request routing book-keeping (route maps, per-expert offsets) causes CPU-side overhead and GPU synchronization points that are not amortized at small batch sizes.
3) Kernel fragmentation (many small kernels) prevents the CUDA scheduler from achieving high SM occupancy; model compiler sometimes emits numerous tiny kernels for expert slices.
4) Attention-sparsity helps but only if we can fuse index math + GEMM into single kernels; otherwise it increases memory footprint and amplifies fragmentation.

Mitigations tried (and results):
- Pre-allocated expert buffers: allocate a contiguous chunk for all expert outputs and reuse across requests. Result: reduces cudaMalloc/cudaFree spikes, p95 down ~18% for MoE tests.
- Fused routing kernel (Triton attempt): combine gating + scatter indices generation into one GPU kernel, emit a single scatter/gather kernel that writes into pre-allocated buffers. Result: reduced memcpy counts and launch count; tokens/sec improved ~22% on A100. Current implementation still has edge cases where expert padding causes extra work.
- Sticky-routing (heuristic): for sequential tokens in the same request, prefer routing to the previous expert if gate scores within a small margin (epsilon). Result: reduces expert hopping and improved cache locality, giving ~9% p95 improvement for long sequences with coherent topics. Tradeoff: potential small quality regression on rare inputs—needs eval.
- Top-1 gating vs Top-2: top-2 gives better quality but doubles scatter/gather complexity. For latency-sensitive tiers we tested top-1 fallbacks with a quality guardrail that switches to top-2 only when gate entropy high. Result: median latency improved ~20% at negligible quality impact on our eval set.
- Precompile dispatch maps for fixed vocab prefixes common in production (prefix caching): amortizes some routing map compute for repeated prefixes, saving ~7% CPU time on steady-state traffic.

Operational recommendations (short-term):
- Use pre-allocated expert pools with a custom allocator (avoid cudaFree/cudaMalloc at request time).
- For latency-sensitive endpoints, default to top-1 gating + quality-guard fallback to top-2 when gate entropy > threshold.
- Expose `sticky_routing_epsilon` configuration per-route so product teams can trade quality vs latency.
- For Qwen/Mistral long-context routes, enable fused block-sparse attention kernels (Triton) only for seq_len >= 2048; fallback to dense kernels below that to avoid index overhead.
- Add telemetry for expert utilization histograms per-tenant so we can decide when expert pruning or expert consolidation is safe.

Medium-term engineering work (prioritized):
- Finish and upstream the fused routing + scatter/gather kernel (PR 1348). This should include careful padding handling to avoid extra zero-work writes.
- Implement per-stream persistent CUDA buffers to avoid host sync. Use CUDA graphs for repeated prefix workloads.
- Implement an expert compaction pass at runtime: if a request touches only K < total_experts, pack those K experts contiguously for that batch to reduce memory footprint and kernel count.
- Compiler-level kernel batching: merge small expert GEMMs across experts when possible (requires graph-level fusion heuristics).

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Quality: sticky-routing and top-1 fallbacks need to be validated against our eval-suite (prompt-specific tests). How big is the QoL/accuracy regression in rare cases?
- Long-tail memory fragmentation: what is the long-term behavior under sustained traffic? Need multi-hour soak tests with realistic mixing.
- Expert pruning policy: can we safely prune low-usage experts per-tenant or per-route and fall back to a denser model for those tenants?
- Interaction with model quantization: does int8/4 quantization amplify fragmentation or change memory alignment in a way that alters routing overhead?

Quick profiling commands & snippets we used:
- torch.profiler example: torch.profiler.profile(activities=[ProfilerActivity.CPU, ProfilerActivity.CUDA], record_shapes=True, with_stack=False) + schedule for warmup/active
- nv-nsight capture: nsight-sys -o trace.qdstrm --capture-range=cpu -- python serve_debug.py --routing-instrumentation
- ncu kernel-level breakdown: ncu --target-processes all --section 'CUDA Runtimes' --launch-skip 1 --launch-count 10 --set fullserve python micro_moe_test.py
- allocator debug: export PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=max_split_size_mb:64; use cupy.get_default_memory_pool().used_bytes() to monitor fragmentation in test harness.

Immediate TODOs:
- [Priya] land expert-pool allocator changes behind feature flag and run 72-hour soak (INF-797).
- [Miguel] finish Triton fused scatter/gather edge-case padding (PR review assigned).
- [Jin] run sticky-routing quality eval on the 3k prompt eval-suite and report regression metrics.
- [Eloise] add expert-util histograms to route telemetry and add Grafana dashboard tile.

Notes to self / rough ideas to explore later:
- Consider hybrid routing where low-entropy prefixes go to a dense adapter to avoid routing entirely for common prefixes.
- Explore a per-tenant compiled expert layout: customers with predictable load could have a smaller packed expert set.
- For attention sparsity, evaluate block-sparse on H100 vs A100 and surface differences; H100 compiler may produce fewer kernels for the same operation.

References / links: see linked_artifacts above for PR + design. Also refer to kernels timeline screenshots in the confluence page.

Unresolved: need to standardize how we report routing overhead in telemetry (percentage vs absolute ms) — currently teams use both, makes comparisons noisy.

End of notes.
